belief: “Bending the truth is fine when it helps me.”
belief_plain: Bending the truth is fine when it helps me.
intro: Have you found that stretching the truth gets you out of trouble or gets you what you want? Do you sometimes lie so smoothly that it surprises you? The information below is intended to help you take a step toward a life without having to cover your tracks, and to find the freedom that comes from knowing God’s word as found in the Bible.
origins: Some people learned early that honesty brought punishment, so they learned to say whatever kept them safe. Others grew up around people who lied freely and rewarded cleverness. Over time, lying can become automatic, especially when it works.
keeps: A lie often solves today’s problem and creates tomorrow’s. Each one has to be remembered and protected, trust erodes, and people begin to doubt me even when I am telling the truth. The loneliness of never being fully known can follow.
teaches: Scripture is clear about honesty and about its rewards. “Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another.” “He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.” And Jesus promised, “Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” Honesty frees us from keeping track of our stories.
key: Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another.
also: He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.
Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.
Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who deal faithfully are His delight.
He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy.
self: A little lie never hurt anyone.
I had to say that to get out of it.
They did not need to know.
I can talk my way out of anything.
Honesty is for people who can afford it.
errors: Treating a lie as small or harmless.
Finding good reasons for something I know is wrong.
Counting the immediate benefit and not the lost trust.
Using others’ behavior to excuse mine.
Feeling safe after a lie and concluding it was right.
Believing I either lie or I lose.
questions: What did I fear would happen if I told the truth?
What has bending the truth cost me in trust?
How many stories am I keeping track of?
What would telling the truth in one small matter look like?
What does Scripture say about integrity?
If someone I love lied to me, how would I feel?
truth: Honesty is safer than I think. Truth builds trust, frees me from keeping track of stories, and lets people know me. I can start by telling the truth in small things, with God’s help.
prayer: Lord, You are the God of truth. Give me courage to be honest, to face what I have hidden, and to build trust that lasts. Amen.
clinical: For counselors: this belief appears in the cognitive model of what clinicians call antisocial personality disorder (Beck, Davis, & Freeman, Cognitive Therapy of Personality Disorders), where views such as “I have to look out for myself,” “others are weak and exploitable,” and “rules do not apply to me” are central. Deceit is often an automatic coping habit; avoid shaming, explore what honesty is feared to cost, and set graded honesty experiments with clear, concrete goals. Expect little spontaneous distress about these beliefs; engagement usually begins with the person’s own goals and costs (relationships, legal trouble, loss of trust), so use collaborative questioning rather than confrontation, set clear boundaries, and keep sessions practical. Assess risk of harm to others, abuse or violence in the home, substance use, and suicide risk; consult or refer as indicated (in the U.S., 988 for crisis). This is an individualized educational formulation, not a DSM criterion or a diagnostic test. Similar presentations can arise from trauma, a hard upbringing, substance use, or other conditions, so careful assessment matters.
morning: Each morning ask: “Where can I tell the plain truth today, even if it costs me something?”
catch: “A little lie will get me out of this.”
hw_truths: I do not have to keep track of stories.
I can be honest in small things first.
People can know me and accept me.
experiments: Tell the plain truth in one small matter today.
Notice each time you want to stretch the truth, and pause for ten seconds.
Admit a small mistake to someone without making an excuse.
Write down one lie you told this week and what the truth would have been.
Ask someone you trust to tell you when you shade things.
Pray Ephesians 4:25 before a hard conversation.
reflect: After listening to one of the four songs, write a sentence about truth setting you free.
newtruth: Honesty is safer than lying. Truth builds trust and sets me free, and I can start in small things.
prayer2: Lord, thank You for the freedom of truth. Give me courage to be honest. Amen.
